title: Service Nexus: VPC stenciling and controlled egress — POC notes
body:
Context and goal:

This doc captures the design thinking, trade-offs, and a short runbook for a customer POC we ran to validate a ‘Service Nexus’ pattern: a small, hardened shared-services VPC + minimal footprint control plane in customer VPCs, with tightly controlled egress and DNS "stenciling" to enforce allowed destinations and reduce data exfil risk for private inference. The customer requirement: run Redwood Private inference inside their account with the ability to reach only a narrow set of vendor endpoints (metrics, S3 artifact pulls, KMS) and to ensure DNS resolution is auditable and can be pointed to either customer resolvers or Redwood-managed resolvers depending on tenancy model.

High-level topology options considered (quick):

1) Direct VPC Peering + private DNS delegation
   - Pros: lowest latency, straightforward route tables, simple for single-region.
   - Cons: scaling across many customer accounts/regions becomes O(n^2) peering, no transitive routing, limited control plane for central egress.

2) Transit Gateway + central egress appliance
   - Pros: scales to many VPCs, central route controls, we can deploy egress proxies/NATs in a central hub.
   - Cons: cost on TGW, slight added hop/latency, additional inter-account roles and attachments.

3) PrivateLink (Interface VPC Endpoints) + DNS forwarding (recommended for narrow-surface POC)
   - Pros: least peripheral attack surface (no route propagation), supports cross-account, caller stays in customer VPC, simpler security model for private endpoints.
   - Cons: per-endpoint ENIs/cost, not suitable for full general internet egress, needs DNS records and conditional forwarding.

Design pattern we validated in POC (Service Nexus, hybrid of 2 + 3):

- Customer VPCs attach to a lightweight shared-services VPC via Transit Gateway for scale. For customers with a single account/regional footprint we validated peering as a fast path option.
- Centralized egress cluster in the shared-services VPC: egress proxy fleet (envoy/mTLS) behind autoscaling and ALB/NLB, and a small NAT pool for non-proxied traffic (artifact S3 pulls).
- DNS stenciling: customer resolver (Route 53 Resolver endpoints) or /etc/resolv.conf stub to forward certain domains to the shared-services resolver. Non-allowed domains resolve to NXDOMAIN locally.
- PrivateLink endpoints exported to the customer account for Redwood-specific control-plane APIs (metrics ingestion, auth/token exchange). These endpoints are only reachable over VPC endpoints and require mTLS and token-based attestation.

DNS control and stenciling details:

- For private inference we need exact behavior for two domain classes:
  * internal vendor domains (metrics.redwood-inference.internal, artifacts.redwood-s3.internal) -> resolved by shared-services Route53 private hosted zone
  * public domains that must be blocked or forwarded (e.g., outbound to general internet) -> blocked via forced NXDOMAIN or resolved to internal blackhole IPs when necessary.

- Implementation alternatives tested:
  A) Route 53 Resolver inbound/outbound endpoints + resolver rules: forward *.redwood-inference.internal to shared-services resolver; block other zones via resolver rule pointing to a blackhole IP.
  B) Customer-side DNS stub resolver (dnsmasq in transit VPC) with allowlist config; simpler to audit and run as container.
  C) Kubernetes cluster-level CoreDNS with policy plugin when workload is in k8s; allows per-namespace whitelists.

- POC decision: use Route 53 Resolver rules for the initial POC and use a small fleet of dnsdist as secondary enforcement (faster iteration for customers that want to host their own).

Egress control (policy and enforcement):

- Two enforcement layers: network (route/NAT/proxy) and application (egress proxy + allowlist).
- Route-level: only advertise routes to shared-services TGW attachment for allowed prefixes. Unadvertised ranges implicitly unreachable.
- Proxy-level: Envoy-based egress mesh that enforces SNI/DNS/HTTP Host allowlist and performs TLS origination where we need to authenticate to downstream services (e.g., signed mTLS).
- Artifact retrieval (S3, model blobs): use VPC Gateway endpoints and a small NAT pool only for cross-account S3 if customer requires. Prefer presigned URLs over general outbound HTTP for better access control.

Service endpoints and access control: concrete items we implemented in the POC

- PrivateLink for auth/ingest: create an NLB in shared-services, create an Interface Endpoint Service, allowlist customer account id via endpoint policy.
- Route53 private hosted zone in shared-services (redwood-internal.local) with NS delegation of subzones to customer VPCs when we need split-horizon semantics.
- IAM/SG: endpoint SGs are locked down to customer subnets/ENI CIDRs and only accept mTLS or short-lived bearer tokens.

Operational runbook (short) - smoke tests we ran during the POC:

1) DNS resolution
   - dig @<resolver> metrics.redwood-inference.internal +short  -> must return private IP
   - dig @<resolver> google.com -> NXDOMAIN or blackhole IP (as per policy)

2) Endpoint connectivity
   - curl --resolve metrics.redwood-inference.internal:<port>:<private-ip> https://metrics.redwood-inference.internal/health -v
   - tcpdump -i eth0 host <shared-services-egress-ip> and curl to validate SNI and mTLS handshake

3) Artifact retrieval
   - aws s3 presign get-object --bucket redwood-artifacts --key model-v1.bin | xargs curl -I

Sample AWS CLI snippets used in the lab (POC):

- create interface endpoint (PE):
  aws ec2 create-vpc-endpoint --vpc-id vpc-012345 --service-name com.amazonaws.vpce.us-west-2.vpce-svc-12345678 --vpc-endpoint-type Interface --subnet-ids subnet-aaa,subnet-bbb --security-group-ids sg-xxxxx

- resolver rule to forward a zone to central resolver:
  aws route53resolver create-resolver-rule --creator-request-id rule1 --domain-name redwood-internal.local --rule-type FORWARD --target-ips Ip=10.2.5.10,Port=53 --resolver-endpoint-id rslvr-out-abc

Performance and cost notes from the POC:

- Transit Gateway adds ~1-3ms median hop compared to direct peering in the same AZ; throughput is dominated by ENI limits on interface endpoints for high-throughput telemetry ingestion.
- PrivateLink costs scale per-ENI; for scale customers evaluate using a small set of regional endpoints + a high-throughput NLB rather than many per-AZ endpoints.
- DNS forwarding adds negligible CPU but adds a small resolution latency (~1–4ms) depending on the resolver chain.

Security and compliance considerations:

- Audit: Route 53 Resolver query logging to S3 + CloudWatch for a 30 day retention (customer requirement varied).
- Egress L4/L7 telemetry: Envoy access logs to central observability, token exchange audit logs retained per customer SLA.
- Key management: allow only customer KMS for any customer-provided secrets; Redwood holds tokens for managed model store only under contractual data handling terms.

POC open questions and next steps:

- How does the customer want split-horizon for third-party CDNs (fast external model pulls) vs blocked external DNS? Need specific domain list.
- Should we provide an optional lightweight customer-side DNS appliance image (AMIs/container) for customers that cannot use R53 Resolver?
- Capacity test: validate PrivateLink ENI scaling under sustained 5000 req/s ingestion for telemetry (next sprint).

Action items (owners):

- Asha: publish Terraform module skeleton for shared-services TGW + Endpoint service (draft by 2025-03-09).
- Liam: capture allowed domain list template and example resolver rules (by 2025-03-05).
- Sofia: run throughput test for Interface Endpoint scaling and report CPU/ENI saturation points (by 2025-03-16).
- Ben: produce a one-page customer-facing diagram and short security spec for the SRE/security review (by 2025-03-12).

Appendix: short checklist for customer POC kickoff

- [ ] Confirm customer account IDs and region list
- [ ] Agree on allowed outbound domains and artifact buckets
- [ ] Confirm KMS key usage and cross-account grants
- [ ] Decide TGW vs peering (based on number of VPCs and cross-account requirements)
- [ ] Set up resolver logs and short retention for initial testing

Notes-to-self style fragments from the workshop (raw):

- "If customer insists on zero TGW cost, peering + PrivateLink can be ok for <3 accounts, otherwise TGW win"
- "Consider offering a managed DNS policy package where we keep a curated allowlist and rotate blackhole responses"
- "Edge-case: customer uses non-AWS DNS that blocks forwarding; fallback is to ship a dnsmasq container in customer kube infra"

End of notes.
